questions.q: Which of the following statements about instruction tuning of a pretrained language model are true?
options: The prompt tokens are masked out of the next-token loss, so only the response tokens are supervised.
It updates the parameters of the base model.
It requires a separately trained reward model.
Training on several different phrasings of the same task improves generalisation to unseen instructions.

questions.q: In prompt tuning, which parameters are updated during training?
options: All the weights of the pretrained model
Only the continuous prompt embeddings prepended to the input, while the model stays frozen
Only the final layer normalisation and the output head
The merge rules of the tokenizer

questions.q: Which capability does Tree-of-Thought (ToT) prompting add over Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting?
options: It fine-tunes the model on reasoning traces before inference.
It maintains several candidate reasoning branches and can backtrack from unpromising ones.
It removes the need for any prompt design.
It guarantees that the final answer is factually correct.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT captured by the POSIX metric for prompt sensitivity?
options: Diversity in the responses produced under intent-preserving prompt variations
Entropy of the distribution of response frequencies
The wall-clock time taken to generate a response
Variance in the log-likelihood assigned to the same response across prompt variations

questions.q: Which conclusion about prompt sensitivity is supported by POSIX measurements across model families?
options: Prompt sensitivity decreases monotonically with parameter count.
A larger model within the same family can still be more prompt sensitive than a smaller one.
Prompt sensitivity is zero for any instruction-tuned model.
All models of the same parameter count have identical prompt sensitivity.

questions.q: Why is alignment performed on top of instruction tuning rather than stopping at instruction tuning?
options: Instruction tuning does not allow the model to follow any instructions at all.
Instruction tuning can still yield fluent, instruction-following responses that humans judge harmful or unacceptable.
Instruction tuning destroys the model's performance on downstream tasks.
Alignment is needed only for models below a few billion parameters.

questions.q: A reward model r(x, y) is trained on preference triples (x, y_w, y_l), where y_w is the preferred response and y_l the rejected one. Using the Bradley-Terry formulation, the training objective maximises:
options: log σ( r(x, y_l) - r(x, y_w) )
log σ( r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l) )
the entropy of the policy distribution
the KL divergence between the policy and the reference model

questions.q: In RLHF the policy is optimised for reward while a KL penalty against a reference policy is applied. What is the primary purpose of that KL term?
options: To make each gradient update cheaper to compute
To keep the optimised policy close to the reference model, so it does not drift into degenerate high-reward behaviour
To increase the entropy of the sampled responses
To remove annotator bias from the preference dataset

questions.q: Which of the following statements about REINFORCE-style policy optimisation for language models are true?
options: The log-derivative trick yields an unbiased estimator of the policy gradient from sampled responses.
Weighting the token-level log-probabilities by an advantage rather than the raw return reduces gradient variance.
Importance ratios are clipped when several updates are taken on samples drawn from an older policy.
The reward function must be differentiable with respect to the model parameters.

questions.q: Let ratio_t = π_new(a_t|s_t) / π_old(a_t|s_t), and let ε > 0 be the clipping parameter. When the token-level advantage A_t is negative, the PPO-CLIP objective at step t reduces to maximising:
options: min( ratio_t, 1 + ε ) A_t
max( ratio_t, 1 - ε ) A_t
min( ratio_t, 1 - ε ) A_t
max( ratio_t, 1 + ε ) A_t
questions.explanation: For A_t < 0, min(r A, clip(r, 1-eps, 1+eps) A) = A * max(r, 1-eps). Only one channel (NALANDA) showed this answer; it matches the derivation.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why a knowledge graph (KG) is a more flexible representation than a traditional relational knowledge base?
options: A KG needs no schema at all, whereas a relational knowledge base always does.
A KG stores entities as nodes joined by typed edges, so heterogeneous relations and multi-hop traversal are represented directly.
A KG stores every fact as a hypergraph, which removes all redundancy.
A KG makes textual sources unnecessary because it stores every possible fact.

questions.q: Entity and relation alignment across knowledge graphs in different languages is a hard problem. Which of the following genuinely contribute to effective alignment?
options: Transliteration and cross-lingual string matching over entity labels
Comparing the neighbourhood structure of candidate entities in the two graphs
Requiring that every alias of an entity appears identically in both graphs
Matching relations purely on the lexical similarity of their names, ignoring context

questions.q: Which of the following are learned jointly in an end-to-end differentiable KGQA system, as opposed to a semantic parsing approach?
options: A dense representation of the natural language question
Embeddings of the entities and relations in the graph
A hand-specified logical form for each question template
The scoring mechanism that selects which node answers the question

questions.q: Which statements correctly describe the local closed-world assumption used when generating negatives for KG training?
options: Triples not present in the graph are treated as false during training.
It is strictly correct, because knowledge graphs are complete by construction.
Some sampled negatives are in fact missing true triples, so the training signal carries label noise.
It removes the need for a separate validation split.

questions.q: A KG completion model is trained with a softmax over entities to model P(o | s, r). Which of the following statements about replacing the full softmax with a sampled one are correct?
options: The exact denominator requires scoring every entity in the graph, which is prohibitively expensive for large KGs.
The true object must be kept in the sampled denominator, otherwise the estimate is biased.
Sampling negatives uniformly tends to produce easy negatives, giving a high-variance training signal.
Sampled softmax removes the need to learn entity embeddings.

questions.q: A model is trained with the pairwise hinge loss max{0, m + f(s', r, o') - f(s, r, o)}, where (s, r, o) is a positive triple, (s', r, o') a sampled negative, m > 0 the margin, and a higher f means a more plausible triple. The loss is strictly positive when:
options: f(s, r, o) ≥ f(s', r, o') + m
f(s, r, o) < f(s', r, o') + m
f(s', r, o') ≥ f(s, r, o) + m
only when m = 0

questions.q: For a single test query, a KG completion model ranks the correct entity 4th out of 100 candidates. What are hits@1, hits@5 and the reciprocal rank for this query?
questions.explanation: Rank 4: hits@1 = 0, hits@5 = 1, reciprocal rank = 1/4.

questions.q: Which statements about filtered evaluation for KG completion are correct?
options: Candidate entities that form known true triples in the training or validation data are removed from the ranked list before the test entity is scored.
It avoids penalising the model for placing a different, genuinely correct answer above the held-out one.
It can only ever lower the reported score compared with the raw setting.
It changes ranking metrics such as MRR and hits@K.

questions.q: Why can TransE not represent a non-trivial symmetric relation?
options: Because the norm of every relation embedding in TransE is constrained to 1.
Because symmetry would require both s + r ≈ o and o + r ≈ s, which forces r ≈ 0 and collapses the relation.
Because the subject and object embeddings would have to be orthogonal.
Because TransE uses complex-valued embeddings that cannot encode symmetry.

questions.q: Which of the following is the RotatE scoring function?
options: f(s, r, o) = ‖ s + r - o ‖
f(s, r, o) = ‖ s ⊙ r - o ‖, where every component of r has modulus 1
f(s, r, o) = s^T M_r o, with M_r a full matrix
f(s, r, o) = - <s, r, o>, the real part of a three-way inner product
questions.explanation: NALANDA and Engineering Study Desk give B; one channel's ticks also matched option D, which is not the RotatE score.

questions.q: In LoRA, the update to a frozen weight matrix W of shape d × k is parameterised as ΔW = B A, with B of shape d × r and A of shape r × k. For d = k = 4096 and rank r = 8, how many trainable parameters does this adapter introduce for that one matrix?
Where do prefix tuning and adapters inject their task-specific parameters in a Transformer?
options: Prefix tuning inserts bottleneck feed-forward modules inside each block, while adapters prepend trainable vectors to the input.
Prefix tuning prepends trainable key and value vectors at every layer, while adapters insert small bottleneck modules inside the blocks.
Both modify only the final output projection, differing in how they initialise it.
Both work purely by altering the attention mask.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about extensions of LoRA are correct?
options: QLoRA trains low-rank adapters on top of a base model quantised to 4 bits.
DyLoRA trains over a range of ranks so that a rank can be selected afterwards without retraining.
AdaLoRA distributes a parameter budget across modules by importance instead of fixing one rank everywhere.
LoRA adapters cannot be folded back into the base weights, so they always add inference latency.

questions.q: Why does unstructured magnitude pruning often fail to deliver a wall-clock speedup even at high sparsity?
options: Because it removes entire attention heads and so changes the output dimension.
Because the surviving weights are scattered irregularly, and dense kernels cannot exploit that sparsity without specialised hardware or sparse formats.
Because the pruned model must be retrained from random initialisation.
Because only bias terms are eligible for removal.

questions.q: What distinguishes quantization-aware training (QAT) from post-training quantization (PTQ)?
options: QAT simulates the quantisation error during training so the weights adapt to it, while PTQ quantises an already trained model using a small calibration set.
QAT is applied only to activations and PTQ only to weights.
PTQ requires more compute than QAT because it retrains every layer.
PTQ can only be applied to models below one billion parameters.

questions.q: In QLoRA, what does double quantization actually quantise a second time?
options: The attention weights, taken down to 1 bit in a second pass.
The gradients, before they are accumulated into the optimiser state.
The quantisation constants themselves, that is the per-block scale factors produced by the first quantisation.
Portions of the model that are reverted to FP16 whenever accuracy drops.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about knowledge distillation for language models are correct?
options: Word-level distillation trains the student to match the teacher's output distribution at each token position.
Sequence-level distillation trains the student on sequences generated by the teacher rather than on per-token distributions alone.
The two can be combined so the student learns both local token probabilities and global sequence structure.
Sequence-level distillation requires the teacher to emit a chain-of-thought explanation for every example.

questions.q: In mechanistic interpretability, what is meant by a circuit?
options: A pipeline that collects and batches training examples for an autoregressive model
A recurrent module inserted into a Transformer to give it additional memory
A subgraph of the network - particular heads, neurons and connections - hypothesised to implement a specific behaviour
An external tool used to adjust parameters after training has finished

questions.q: In-context copying of the pattern [A][B] ... [A] → [B] is attributed to induction heads. Which description matches the mechanism?
options: A single head that attends to punctuation to segment the sequence into repeated units
A previous-token head that writes information about the preceding token, composed with a later head that attends to the token following the earlier occurrence of A and copies it
A feed-forward sub-layer that raises the probability of any token seen earlier in the context
A head that masks future positions so that repeated tokens cannot be attended to
questions.explanation: Single-choice; one detection also matched C, but all other sources give B.

questions.q: In the transformer circuits framing, what do the QK and OV circuits respectively determine for an attention head?
options: QK determines where the head attends, OV determines what is read from the attended position and written to the output.
QK determines what is written to the output, OV determines where the head attends.
Both determine how positional information is encoded.
Both are normalisation terms that keep the attention scores in a fixed range.

questions.q: Which statements correctly characterise the DistMult model for knowledge graph completion?
options: Each relation is parameterised by a full D × D matrix, which lets it capture asymmetric relations.
The relation is represented by a diagonal matrix, so the score is a multiplicative interaction of the entity embeddings.
Because the diagonal form makes the score symmetric in the subject and object, it cannot distinguish a relation from its inverse.
DistMult can only be evaluated on knowledge graphs whose relations are all symmetric.

questions.q:
In DistMult the score of a triple is the sum over dimensions of the element-wise product of the subject, relation and object embeddings. Given:

s = [1, 2, 0], r = [2, -1, 3], o = [3, 1, 4]

What are the scores of (s, r, o) and of the reversed triple (o, r, s)?
options: 4 and 4
4 and -4
4 and 12
6 and 4
questions.explanation: Score(s,r,o) = 1*2*3 + 2*(-1)*1 + 0*3*4 = 4; DistMult is symmetric, so the reversed triple also scores 4.

questions.q: Which statements about the ComplEx extension of DistMult are true?
options: It moves the embeddings into the complex domain and takes the complex conjugate of the object embedding in the score.
It replaces multiplicative interaction with element-wise addition of real-valued vectors.
Setting the imaginary part of a relation embedding to zero recovers a symmetric, DistMult-like score.
Every entity embedding must have unit norm for the model to be valid.
questions.explanation: Four sources give A and C; Engineering Study Desk ticked only A.

questions.q: What is the main modification SimplE makes to DistMult-style models in order to handle asymmetric relations?
options: It replaces the entity embeddings with fixed random vectors.
It gives every entity two embeddings, one for its subject role and one for its object role, and learns an embedding for each inverse relation.
It constrains the relation tensor to rank one.
It samples negatives for only half of the training triples.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of a factorised representation such as DistMult or ComplEx for a large knowledge graph?
options: It forces every relation in the graph to be symmetric.
It stores each entity as a one-hot vector, which simplifies nearest-neighbour search.
It collapses the graph into a single scalar summary.
It replaces the full adjacency tensor with low-rank factors, which cuts the parameter count and lets the model generalise to unseen triples.

questions.q: How is a 3D knowledge graph tensor of shape |E| × |R| × |E| commonly reshaped into a matrix factorisation problem?
options: The entire tensor is flattened into a 1D array and factorised with SVD.
Each subject-relation pair is collapsed into a single index along one axis, while the objects remain along the other axis.
The subject dimension is repeated until it matches the relation dimension.
The relation axis is discarded and the remaining two axes are factorised.

questions.q: Which property of hierarchical relations motivates specialised embedding geometries rather than standard Euclidean KG embeddings?
options: Symmetry: (A, is-a, B) implying (B, is-a, A)
The frequent presence of cycles in a taxonomy
Transitivity: (camel, is-a, mammal) and (mammal, is-a, animal) implying (camel, is-a, animal)
The high dimensionality of the entity embeddings

questions.q: Which statements about hyperbolic (Poincaré ball) embeddings for hierarchical data are correct?
options: The volume available grows exponentially with radius, which matches the exponential growth in the number of nodes at each level of a tree.
Distances grow slowly near the centre and increase sharply towards the boundary, so depth in a hierarchy maps naturally onto radius.
Every node must be placed exactly on the boundary of the unit ball.
They give arbitrarily low distortion for any graph, not only tree-like ones.
questions.explanation: Four sources give A and B; Engineering Study Desk ticked only A.

questions.q: Why can a partial-order approach such as order embeddings suit 'is-a' relations better than a purely distance-based one?
options: It encodes the ancestor-descendant relation directly as a coordinate-wise inequality or containment.
It guarantees the full transitive closure of the hierarchy is recovered without any training.
It represents sibling and ancestor pairs as negatively correlated vectors.
It replaces symmetric pairwise distance with an asymmetric notion of ordering, which matches the asymmetry of is-a.

questions.q: Which limitation of axis-aligned cone embeddings do box embeddings address?
options: Cones cannot represent containment at all, whereas boxes can.
A cone has the same measure regardless of how broad or narrow it is, so the size of a category cannot be read off its region, whereas a box has a finite volume that can.
Cones require all sibling categories to share an apex.
Cones cannot be trained with gradient descent.

questions.q:
Which of the following statements about bias in large language models are correct?
1. Stereotypical associations can appear in model outputs even when no one involved in building the model intended them.
2. Bias enters only during fine-tuning and never from the pretraining corpus.
3. Biased outputs can cause real-world harm by reinforcing discrimination against particular groups.
4. A model that scores highly on standard accuracy benchmarks is necessarily free of bias.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
1, 3 and 4

questions.q: In the StereoSet framework, what does a Stereotype Score (ss) of 50 indicate?
options: The model refuses half of all prompts that mention a demographic group.
The model chooses the stereotypical and the anti-stereotypical association equally often, which is the ideal value for this metric.
Half of the model's completions are meaningless rather than meaningful.
The model's accuracy on the stereotype detection task is 50 percent.

questions.q:
StereoSet reports the idealised CAT score as:
icat = lms × min(ss, 100 - ss) / 50

For a model with a language modelling score lms = 80 and a stereotype score ss = 70, what is its icat?

Which of the following are recognised sources of bias in large language models?

1. Skewed selection of training data, over-representing some topics or communities.
2. Reliance on older corpora, producing temporal bias against current usage and norms.
3. Over-representation of low-resource languages, producing what is termed linguistic inversion.
4. Dominance of a few high-resource languages, producing cultural bias in what the model treats as default.
options: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the 'regard' metric?
options: A measure of how well a model can explain its own decision process.
The perplexity of a model on demographically sensitive text.
A classifier-assigned label capturing the attitude that generated text expresses towards a demographic group.
The proportion of occasions on which a model spontaneously corrects discriminatory language.

questions.q: In bias mitigation with adversarial triggers, what is the aim of prepending a specially chosen token sequence to the prompt?
options: To fine-tune the model parameters so the bias is removed permanently.
To overwrite the model's prior knowledge and effectively reset it.
To exploit the model's existing distribution so that biased associations in the continuation are neutralised or reversed.
To randomise the token order so the model becomes robust to input perturbation.

questions.q: Which steps make up the approach of improving response safety through in-context learning?
options: Retrieving safety demonstrations that resemble the incoming user query.
Fine-tuning the model on newly labelled data after each generation.
Including the retrieved demonstrations in the prompt as examples that guide the response.
Sampling many responses and returning whichever opinion appears most often.

questions.q: Which statements about the effect of high-resource (HRL) and low-resource languages (LRL) on model training are correct?
options: LRLs tend to show higher performance because they are spoken by smaller populations.
HRLs contribute far more training data, so the model can overfit to the cultural perspectives carried in them.
LRLs are under-represented, so the model captures their cultural nuances poorly.
The dominance of HRLs is self-reinforcing, since better performance attracts more data and more investment.

questions.q: What does counterfactual data augmentation mean as a debiasing technique?
options: Generating synthetic examples with a second model and filtering them by a reward score.
Creating additional training examples by swapping demographic terms in existing text, so that associations are balanced across groups.
Removing every sentence that mentions a demographic group from the training corpus.
Adding a penalty term to the loss whenever the model generates a demographic term.

questions.q: The idea of a 'Responsible LLM' is presented as addressing which of the following?
options: Bias and fairness alone
A set of concerns spanning fairness, explainability, robustness, privacy and security
Only the trade-off between training cost and carbon footprint
The deployment of purely rule-based output filters
